title: Pawn majorities: making a passed pawn
summary: Turn an extra pawn on one wing into a passed pawn, and know why the queenside majority is an endgame asset.

steps.md:
A **pawn majority** is more pawns than the opponent on one wing (for example 3 against 2 on the queenside), even when material is level overall. Any healthy majority can create a **passed pawn**.

- A **queenside majority** is valuable in endgames: the passed pawn it creates is far from the kings, so it decoys the enemy king (outside passed pawn).
- A **kingside majority** usually supports a middlegame attack or a central passer.

Technique: advance the **candidate pawn** (the one with no enemy pawn in front of it) first, supported by its neighbours; avoid advancing a pawn that can be blocked by one enemy pawn holding two of yours.

steps.question: White has pawns a2, b2, c2 against Black's a7, b7. Which pawn is the "candidate" (the one that becomes passed)?
choices: The c-pawn: no black pawn stands in front of it
steps.explain: The c-pawn faces no enemy pawn on its file, so it will become passed after b-pawn and c-pawn exchanges against a7/b7. Typical sequence: b4, c4, c5 (or b5) to force the passer. Pushing the a-pawn first often lets ...a5 or ...b5 hold two pawns with one.

steps.md: White to move. Material is level, but White has **3 against 2 on the queenside**, while the kingside is locked (g3/h4 against g6/h5). White will create a passed pawn on the queenside; the black king must run to stop it, and the white king then attacks the kingside pawns.

steps.question: In the diagram, what is White's first priority?
choices: Activate the king (Ke3/Kf3 towards the centre and kingside), then use the majority
Offer a draw: material is equal
steps.explain: In pawn endings **king activity** first, then the majority. Engine check: Kf3 or Ke3 win most convincingly; rushing pawns is less precise. The majority will tie the black king to the queenside later.

steps.prompt: Win with the queenside majority: activate your king, create a passed pawn, and promote it (the engine defends).
steps.explain: The plan: king to the centre, create a passer with the candidate c-pawn (b4, c4, c5), use it to decoy the black king, then invade on the kingside or escort the passer.

steps.question: Why is a queenside majority often better than a kingside one in the endgame (with both sides castled short)?
choices: The passed pawn it creates is far from both kings, so the defending king is drawn away from the other wing
It is not; they are equal
steps.explain: Distance is the point: an outside passed pawn deflects the enemy king. The same logic is why pawn endgames with an outside passer are usually won (stage-3 lesson).

steps.md: **Retrieval check.** Define a pawn majority and a candidate pawn. In the diagram, what came first: king or pawns? Typical error: advancing the majority so that one enemy pawn blocks two of yours.

sources: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), the queenside majority
de la Villa, 100 Endgames You Must Know (New in Chess, 2008)
